subject: Banking
title: HSBC and the Drug Cartels
description: A quick win: understand HSBC and the Drug Cartels.

hook.text: HSBC laundered $881 million for Mexican drug cartels. The bank designed deposit boxes sized for cartel cash.

buildup.text: Between 2006 and 2010, HSBC's Mexican branch moved billions in suspicious cash.

discovery.text: HSBC also processed transactions for countries under US sanctions: Iran, Libya, Sudan, and Burma.

twist.text: No HSBC executive went to prison. The bank paid $1.9 billion — about five weeks of profit.

climax.text: HSBC proved that banks can launder cartel money and survive. Too big to fail means too big to jail.

punchline.text: $881 million in cartel cash. Five weeks of profit as a fine. No one jailed.

quiz.question: Why didn't HSBC executives go to prison for money laundering?
options: The bank was deemed too big to prosecute criminally

details.summary: HSBC allowed Mexican drug cartels and sanctioned nations to launder at least $881 million through its US operations, paying a $1.9 billion fine in 2012 but avoiding criminal prosecution of any executives.
details.whyItMatters: HSBC's case became the defining example of too-big-to-jail, where prosecutors feared that criminally charging a global bank could destabilize the financial system, prioritizing stability over justice.
takeaways: Drug cartels physically deposited cash through HSBC Mexico branches
The bank also processed transactions for sanctioned countries like Iran
No HSBC executives were criminally prosecuted despite admitted violations

faq.question: How did HSBC help drug cartels launder money?
faq.answer: HSBC Mexico accepted large cash deposits from cartel-linked businesses with minimal checks. The bank's lax compliance allowed billions in suspicious bulk cash to flow from Mexico to the US banking system.

faq.question: Why were no HSBC executives charged with crimes?
faq.answer: The Department of Justice used a deferred prosecution agreement, arguing that criminal charges against HSBC could destabilize international banking. This decision was widely criticized as creating a two-tier justice system.
